tailMarker.anomalyNote: The marker is a PRESERVATIVE at rank 18, one rank ahead of Parfum @19, in a 21-entry list. That gives the cohort's second-longest above-tail segment and demotes almost nothing — only Parfum and its two declared allergens sit in the tail. No §3.1 anomaly. Consequence worth noting: a Naturkosmetik formula with a short preservative system and a short fragrance block gets nearly its whole list credited, while conventional formulas with early Parfum lose theirs. The formula carries a broad and genuinely material payload — three proteins, five humectants — but §9.1 measures structural conditioning intensity, not payload breadth, and on that axis this is a single-cationic, single-lipid formula. E2 ceiling: comparative structural intensity potential, not measured treatment performance.

conditioningLevel.derivation: S1 = NOT satisfied (one cationic species). S2 = satisfied (Cetearyl Alcohol @2). S3 = NOT satisfied (one lipid, against a required two; the two fatty alcohols are excluded from the lipid count by S3's own wording). Count = 1 of 3.

Confidence `moderate` by §9.1's own rule: high confidence requires ≥2 signals pointing the same way.

Step 3, tested in order: `repair` requires a distinct R5 protein/peptide film route — satisfied by three species. The hierarchy resolves the primary slot at step 3. `moisture` does not take the PRIMARY slot: §9.5.2 tests moisture at step 4, explicitly 'after repair/curl/colour/lightness because D5 requires that no richer special-purpose route wins'. A richer special-purpose route won. §9.5.3 criterion 3 then routes moisture to the secondary slot, which is exactly what happened.

This is the cohort's one live conflict between two binding rules, and it is recorded rather than resolved unilaterally. §9.5.1 states that exact-product claims MAY break a genuinely `dual_supported` tie. The verdict here IS `dual_supported`. The product's own name and lead claim are hydration-first. So §9.5.1 would hand the primary slot to `moisture`, while §9.5.2's ordering hands it to `repair`. I applied the deterministic hierarchy, because a formula-first standard cannot let a claim override a step order without saying so. See AP-08-TIEBREAK.

`smoothing` does not apply: reached only at step 6, after a step-3 route cleared. Its claim ('glättet die Haarstruktur & wirkt Frizz entgegen') has no architecture behind it — no silicone, no substantive polymer, one lipid at rank 17.
`general` does not apply: a differentiator cleared.
counterSignals: Confidence is held at `moderate` specifically because of AP-08-TIEBREAK: a reviewer applying §9.5.1's tie-break in good faith reaches `moisture` as primary and `repair` as secondary — the same two values in the opposite order. This is a predictable blind-lane disagreement and should be adjudicated as a rule question, not scored as a reviewer error.
The 'Frizz' and 'glättet' claims were consulted and refused corroborating force, having no architecture to corroborate.

focusCareVerdict.note: The formula genuinely supports both directions: three distinct hydrolyzed proteins at ranks 7–9 (M2) and five distinct humectants across four families above the tail (M5), on disjoint mechanisms with almost no M1 richness to confuse either with. This is the cohort's only `dual_supported` verdict. claim_role is recorded as `tie_breaker` because §9.5.1 makes claims eligible to break exactly this kind of tie — and the product's name and lead claim ('Intense Hydration', 'Feuchtigkeitsbooster') would break it toward `moisture`. The claim was NOT applied, because §9.5.2's deterministic step order had already resolved the primary slot to `repair` at step 3. Both rules are binding and they point different ways; the conflict is escalated in AP-08-TIEBREAK rather than settled here.

adjudicationPoints.title: §9.5.1's claim tie-break and §9.5.2's step order collide on the cohort's only dual_supported product
adjudicationPoints.body: §9.5.1 (binding, adapted from Shampoo Focus v1.5) says exact-product claims MAY break a genuinely `dual_supported` tie. §9.5.2 (deterministic hierarchy) tests `repair` at step 3 and `moisture` at step 4, so a formula that supports both never presents a tie for a claim to break — the step order always resolves it toward repair. On this product the two rules give different primaries: hierarchy says repair, claim tie-break says moisture. I applied the hierarchy and flagged it. This is not a hypothetical: it is a predictable blind-lane disagreement on a real product, and whichever way Nick rules, the losing sentence should be amended so the next reviewer is not left to choose. My recommendation, for Nick's decision and not adopted here: keep the hierarchy authoritative and narrow §9.5.1's tie-break to cases where two routes clear at the SAME step (e.g. two step-3 routes), since a formula-first standard should not let packaging reorder its own hierarchy.

adjudicationPoints.title: §9.7's specialist damage_fit branch is unreachable without conditioning_level `high`
adjudicationPoints.body: This product carries the cohort's strongest protein film route — three distinct hydrolyzed proteins at consecutive above-tail ranks 7–9 — and earns repair_support_level `medium`, which §9.7 names as specialist qualifier (a). It still lands on healthy + moderately_damaged, because the specialist row is available only under conditioning_level `high`, and this lean Naturkosmetik formula is structurally `moderate`. Meanwhile #05, a rich almond-milk mask with two proteins, reaches the specialist row purely because its lipid stack pushed conditioning_level to `high`. The table therefore makes richness a precondition for a damage-specialist prior. That may be the intended conservatism — §9.7's mask delta warns that a large specialist bucket would mean the test is leaking — but as written the specialist qualifier list is misleading, because qualifier (a) cannot act on its own.

adjudicationPoints.title: The tail-marker rule systematically credits more of a Naturkosmetik list than a conventional one
adjudicationPoints.body: This product's earliest tail-class ingredient is Potassium Sorbate at rank 18 of 21, so 17 of 21 entries are credited. #11's earliest tail-class ingredient is a colourant at rank 7 of 30, so 6 of 30 are credited. The difference is driven by formulation philosophy — short preservative systems, short fragrance blocks, no colourants — rather than by anything about care payload. The rule is reproducible and defensible, but reviewers should know that above-tail segment length correlates with brand positioning, and that cross-product comparisons of 'how much is above the tail' are not comparing like with like.
